newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin heart clinic a far cry from West.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin heart clinic a far cry from West.

text.p: Boris Yeltsin is getting the best Russia has to offer for the heart operation he is undergoing on Tuesday.
But although the elite Cardiology Research Centre where he is having the surgery boasts some of the best doctors in the world, it is a far cry from the glistening hospitals of the West.

Set in a windswept wasteland near the motorway which rings Moscow, the whitewashed clinic stands alongside the site of a vast, unfinished hospital where building stopped with the collapse of communism and is only just getting going again.
The cardio-clinic was completed in the mid-80s, but it has preserved a distinctly Soviet air.
Long, gloomy corridors are lined with the wood panelling which is a hallmark of establishments designed for the privileged in communist society.
"What are you doing in here? Get out," shouts a plump nurse in the intensive care department in the favoured tone of officialdom throughout the former Soviet Union.
When her boss, the Head of Anaesthesia and Intensive Care appears, she softens her tone, but still insists. "But we've just washed the floor," she moans.
"Well you'll just have to do it again," says Mikhail Lepilin, adding firmly. "Do I have to repeat myself?"
The intensive care ward, where doctors said Yeltsin was to recover from several hours in the operating theatre, can take five patients, although Yeltsin is certain to be alone.
"Everyone comes here, even top people," said Lepilin. The linoleum floor is clean, but worn, and the equipment and the wooden nurse's desk are old.

The process of anaesthetising the 65-year-old president is one of the most sensitive parts of the operation. For someone of that age, and with a history of problems with other organs, doctors have to be sure to get the dose just right.
The operating theatre -- where Yeltsin is attended upon by about a dozen medical staff -- is a circular room lined in shining steel with doors opening onto anterooms.
It looks much like its counterparts in the West and is full of equipment from Germany, Sweden, France and Britain.
"The theatre was built in 1984, but the equipment is newer," said Lepilin.

There is a heart-and-lung machine which will take over when Yeltsin's own heart is stopped for the operation, a machine to reduce his body temperature to limit the trauma of surgery, and another to collect spilt blood to be pumped back into him.

A video camera over the table can transmit pictures to trainee doctors -- or in this case probably -- Yeltsin's anxious aides and top U.S. surgeon Michael DeBakey, who will consult on, but not perform the operation.
The staff are particularly proud of the multiple microscope which pulls out on an arm over the patient.
"This is a Russian invention. It allows much greater magnification," said Lepilin, explaining that Western surgeons wore individual magnifying spectacles.
Nevertheless, the clinic's chief cardiologist Renat Akchurin, who is in charge of Yeltsin's operation, has brought equipment from DeBakey's clinic in Houston to help.
One former patient, speaking soon after his own bypass operation, said Yeltsin had nothing to fear. "I've tested the room out for you, everyone here is wonderful," he said.
